name: Guanyin Bodhisattva
domain: Great Compassion, Savior from Suffering, Hearer of Cries
description: No matter what you believe, most people in Taiwan have cried out 'Guanyin Ma, protect me' at the hardest moment of their lives. Guanyin — Guanyin Bodhisattva, known here as Guanyin Ma or Guanyin Fozu, and in the West as the Goddess of Mercy or Avalokitesvara — is the deity you recognize before you know her name: robed in white, holding a vase of pure water and a willow branch, radiating a calm that crosses every line between Buddhism, Taoism, and folk belief. She is the most barrier-free of all the bodhisattvas. Her duty comes down to four words: to rescue those who suffer. The sutras say she has thirty-two manifestations and goes wherever there is pain — regardless of your faith, regardless of what you have done. One surprising note of history: in Indian Buddhism, Avalokitesvara was originally male, and only after arriving in China, around the Northern and Southern Dynasties, did the image gradually turn feminine, settling by the Tang and Song into the white-robed, motherly figure we know today. Scholars offer many explanations, but the most poetic is simple — in the Chinese heart, the highest form of compassion is a mother's love. Step into almost any temple in Taiwan, whoever the main deity may be, and chances are you'll find Guanyin somewhere inside.
story:
What moves people most about Guanyin is that she refuses to give up. Legend says she had already earned the right to become a Buddha — the ultimate goal of Buddhist practice — yet she made a vow: as long as a single being still suffers, she will not enter Buddhahood but will remain in the world to help. This is what the sutras mean when they call her the one who 'hears the cries of the world and comes to save': the instant anyone calls out in suffering, she is already on her way.

Taiwanese love to tell a modern version. A man falls into the sea and screams for Guanyin to save him. A boat comes by — he waves it off, waiting for a miracle. A helicopter comes — he waves that off too. He drowns, and in the afterlife he asks her: 'I called out so loudly. Why didn't you save me?' Guanyin replies: 'The boat and the helicopter — I sent them both.'

The lesson is very Taiwanese: divine help rarely arrives looking divine. More often it's the opportunity sitting right in front of you — and whether it works depends on whether you're willing to reach out and take it.

temples.name: Manka Longshan Temple
temples.deityStory: Manka Longshan Temple is Taipei's most famous ancient temple. During WWII, the temple was bombed and the main hall destroyed, but the Guanyin statue remained miraculously unharmed.

temples.name: Linkou Zhulinshan Guanyin Temple
temples.deityStory: Dedicated to the Eighteen-Armed Guanyin, this is a major religious center in the Linkou/Taoyuan area, known for its grand architecture and beautiful gardens.

associatedTemples: Manka Longshan Temple (Wanhua District, Taipei City)
Linkou Zhulinshan Guanyin Temple (Linkou District, New Taipei City)
Qingshui Ziyun Yan (Qingshui District, Taichung City)
Neimen Zizhu Temple (Neimen District, Kaohsiung City)
worship: What to pray for: peace and health, protection from disaster, the safety of your children — but what Guanyin does best is 'peace of mind.' When something is lodged in your heart that you can't get past, praying to her helps in a way that's hard to describe. And it's simple to do: offer fresh flowers, fruit, and clear tea, put your palms together and silently recite 'Namo Guanshiyin Pusa' three times, then talk to her the way you'd confide in a grandmother, laying out your troubles slowly. The simpler the offering the better — Guanyin cares nothing for spectacle. There is only one taboo, and you must never forget it: Guanyin is vegetarian, so the offerings must contain no meat. Chicken, pork, or fish before her altar is a grave disrespect. Around her birthday on the 19th of the second lunar month, temples like Longshan are at their busiest — a fine time to go and feel the atmosphere.
festivals: Guanyin has three major celebration days: birthday (19th of 2nd lunar month), enlightenment day (19th of 6th lunar month), and renunciation day (19th of 9th lunar month). On these occasions, temples hold vegetarian feasts, sutra chanting sessions, and "liberation of life" ceremonies (releasing animals). Longshan Temple in Taipei sees enormous crowds on these days. The pilgrimage to Guanyin Mountain (Guanyinshan) in New Taipei City is a popular folk tradition, combining religious devotion with hiking. Guanyin worship transcends religious boundaries — she is perhaps the only deity equally revered by Buddhists, Taoists, and folk believers in Taiwan.

name: Shakyamuni Buddha
domain: Founder of Buddhism, Teacher of the Three Realms, Symbol of Compassion and Wisdom
description:
Twenty-five hundred years ago, on a moonlit night, a prince mounted a white horse and slipped away from his sleeping wife and newborn son, never once looking back. He was Shakyamuni Buddha — known to Taiwanese as Fozu, Shizun, or Rulai Fo — the founder of Buddhism, born Siddhartha Gautama, crown prince of Kapilavastu in ancient India (in present-day Nepal). At twenty-nine, on his excursions through the four city gates, he came face to face with the realities of old age, sickness, and death, and resolved to renounce his royal life in search of a way beyond suffering. After six years of ascetic striving, he attained enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree and spent the next forty-nine years teaching the Dharma.

In Taiwan, Shakyamuni is the central object of veneration across every Mahayana tradition. Four great modern organizations shape the island's Buddhist landscape — Fo Guang Shan (founded by Master Hsing Yun), Dharma Drum Mountain (Master Sheng Yen), Tzu Chi (Master Cheng Yen), and Chung Tai Chan Monastery — and however their styles differ, all four honor Shakyamuni as their root teacher.

One distinction is worth carrying through the temple door, since newcomers so often blur it: Shakyamuni is the historical teacher who actually lived in this world; Amitabha Buddha presides over the separate cosmic realm of the Western Pure Land; and Guanyin is a bodhisattva of compassion who has not yet become a Buddha. Taiwanese temples frequently enshrine all three side by side. Buddha's Birthday — known internationally as Vesak — is the most important Buddhist holiday in Taiwan; in 2026 it falls on May 5, the 8th day of the 4th lunar month.
story:
Many legends cluster around the Buddha's life. It's said that the moment he was born he took seven steps, a lotus blossoming beneath each one. But the real story begins outside the palace walls. On the day of the four excursions, the young prince saw a stooped old man, a groaning invalid, and a cold and rigid corpse — and last, a wandering ascetic with steady, peaceful eyes. In that instant, all his wealth and comfort lost their weight.

At twenty-nine, on a moonlit night, he mounted his white horse Kanthaka and, with his charioteer Channa beside him, left the city behind — the Great Renunciation. Six years of severe asceticism followed, until he was starved to skin and bone and understood at last that torturing the body could never purchase awakening. At the bank of the Nairanjara River he accepted a bowl of milk-rice from the cowherd girl Sujata, and with his strength restored he sat beneath a pippala tree — the Bodhi tree — and vowed not to rise until he had attained enlightenment. Legend says the demon-king Mara sent his daughters and his armies to break his concentration, and the Buddha subdued them all.

Before dawn, he saw clear through to the truths of dependent origination and the Four Noble Truths, and became the Buddha — the Awakened One. For the next forty-nine years he walked the Ganges plain teaching the Dharma, his listeners ranging from kings to butchers, until at last he passed serenely into final nirvana between two sala trees at Kushinagar.

temples.name: Dharma Drum Mountain World Center for Buddhist Education
temples.deityStory: Founded by Master Sheng Yen, Dharma Drum Mountain is one of the Four Great Mountains of Taiwanese Buddhism. The Main Hall enshrines Shakyamuni Buddha, emphasizing 'Spiritual Environmentalism' and the building of a Pure Land on Earth.

temples.name: Kaohsiung Fo Guang Shan Monastery
temples.deityStory: Founded by Master Hsing Yun, Fo Guang Shan is the largest Buddhist monastery in Taiwan. Its Main Hall houses huge statues of the Buddha. It is dedicated to promoting 'Humanistic Buddhism' worldwide.

associatedTemples: Dharma Drum Mountain (Jinshan District, New Taipei City)
Fo Guang Shan (Dashu District, Kaohsiung City)
Chung Tai Chan Monastery (Puli Township, Nantou County)
worship: Worshipping Fozu calls for no lavish meats — quite the opposite. The offerings are simply clear incense, fresh flowers, and fruit, all vegetarian; keeping to a meat-free offering is the most basic rule of all. To pay respects, join your palms and make three bows, or the full three kneelings and nine kowtows, silently reciting 'Namo Original Teacher Shakyamuni Buddha,' or chant the Heart Sutra or the Great Compassion Mantra. Buddhism holds that sincerity is what makes an offering meaningful, so the simpler the offering the better — it's the heart that counts. To pray for blessings, most temples keep 'lamps of light' that you can dedicate. As for where to go: Fo Guang Shan emphasizes Humanistic Buddhism, Dharma Drum Mountain centers on meditation, Tzu Chi is known for its charity, and Chung Tai focuses on Chan meditation education. Each of the four great mountains has its own character — simply choose the one that suits you.
festivals:
Shakyamuni Buddha has three major feast days in Taiwan, collectively referred to in Chinese as the "Three Great Buddhist Festivals" (佛教三大節日):

**Buddha's Birthday (Bathing the Buddha)**: 8th day of the 4th lunar month — **May 5 in 2026**. Temples hold the "Bathing the Buddha" ceremony, in which devotees pour fragrant water over a small standing Buddha statue, symbolizing the purification of the mind. Fo Guang Shan's celebration is the largest, drawing tens of thousands of participants. Tzu Chi traditionally combines Buddha's Birthday with Mother's Day and Tzu Chi Day into a single "Three-in-One" celebration that emphasizes gratitude to parents.

**Buddha's Renunciation Day**: 8th day of the 2nd lunar month, commemorating Prince Siddhartha's Great Renunciation. Temples typically hold sutra recitations and dharma talks.

**Buddha's Enlightenment Day (Laba Festival, 臘八)**: 8th day of the 12th lunar month. On this day, temples cook "Laba congee" — a porridge of rice, beans, nuts, lotus seeds, and other grains — to share with devotees, recalling the bowl of milk-rice offered to the Buddha by the cowherd girl Sujata just before his enlightenment.

Some temples also observe the 15th day of the 2nd lunar month as the Buddha's parinirvana day, with memorial services.

name: Amitabha Buddha
domain: Rebirth in the Pure Land, Pure Land Faith, Removal of Karmic Obstacles
description: Taiwanese say 'Amituofo' to greet each other, to give thanks, even to sigh in exasperation — when a Buddha's name turns into everyday speech, you can imagine how deeply it has spread. Amitabha Buddha, also known as the Buddha of Infinite Life, the Buddha of Infinite Light, and the Welcoming Buddha, is the lord of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhavati). The Pure Land school's practice of 'Buddha-name recitation' is beautifully simple: sincerely believe and aspire, chant 'Namo Amituofo,' and at the moment of death the Buddha himself will come to welcome you into the Western Pure Land. It asks for no profound scholarship — a single name that anyone can recite — and that is exactly why it has become the most widely practiced form of Buddhism in Taiwan. From the 'Buddha-Seven' retreats and daily devotions in the temples to the recitation machines humming at an elder's bedside, this name is chanted across the island day and night. Together with Guanyin and Mahasthamaprapta, Amitabha forms the 'Three Sages of the West,' and he is the deepest support Taiwanese lean on when they face life and death.
story:
The Infinite Life Sutra tells that countless ages ago there was a king who, on hearing the Dharma, was so profoundly moved that he made a startling choice: he set down his entire kingdom and became a monk named Dharmakara. Before the Buddha Lokeshvararaja he made forty-eight great vows, and the most crucial is the eighteenth — the 'Vow of Ten Recitations': that any being who sincerely believes and aspires to be born in his land, even reciting his name just ten times at the moment of death, will be welcomed there without fail; and if this vow went unfulfilled, he swore not to become a Buddha.

After immeasurable eons of practice, every one of the forty-eight vows was fulfilled, and Dharmakara attained Buddhahood as Amitabha. The Western Pure Land raised by the power of his vows is a realm of golden ground, jeweled ponds where lotuses bloom in full, and celestial mandarava flowers drifting from the sky — a place where all suffering has ceased. A king traded a visible kingdom for a Pure Land that catches every being who calls — which is why, for a thousand years, so many have spoken his name in their final moment.

temples.name: Taipei Nung Chan Monastery
temples.deityStory: Nung Chan Monastery is the birthplace of Dharma Drum Mountain, founded by Master Sheng Yen. Its celebrated 'Water-Moon Dharma Hall' — a striking modernist structure of exposed concrete — features a wall inscribed with the Diamond Sutra reflected in a tranquil pool. The monastery regularly hosts seven-day Buddha-name recitation retreats and meditation programs.

temples.name: Kaohsiung Fo Guang Shan
temples.deityStory: Founded by Master Hsing Yun, Fo Guang Shan is one of Taiwan's largest Buddhist monasteries. The Great Buddha Land features a towering statue of Amitabha Buddha radiating light across the grounds. Fo Guang Shan promotes 'Humanistic Buddhism' and houses the Buddha Memorial Center, monastic colleges, and facilities for international visitors.

associatedTemples: Taipei Nung Chan Monastery (Beitou, Taipei City)
Fo Guang Shan (Dashu, Kaohsiung City)
worship: Offerings to Amitabha are plain: fresh flowers, fruit, clean water, and clear incense — never meat. The core practice is 'reciting the Buddha's name': saying 'Namo Amituofo' over and over, aloud or silently, often counted on a string of prayer beads, until the name is woven into daily life. Many Taiwanese Buddhists chant the Amitabha Sutra as a daily devotion and dedicate the merit to their karmic creditors across all lifetimes. To go deeper, you can join a temple 'Buddha-Seven' — seven days of concentrated recitation in pursuit of a state of single-minded, undistracted focus. And when an elder passes away, the chanting-relay team takes turns through the night reciting the Buddha's name to see them off — one of the gentlest farewell rites in Taiwan.
festivals: Amitabha Buddha's birthday on the 17th day of the 11th lunar month is marked by 'Buddha-Seven' retreats (Fo Qi) — intensive seven-day sessions of continuous Buddha-name recitation aimed at achieving 'single-minded focus.' Major monasteries across Taiwan host these retreats, drawing thousands of participants. During the Ghost Month Yulanpen ceremonies in the 7th lunar month, Amitabha's name is also chanted extensively to guide departed souls toward rebirth in the Pure Land.

name: Kshitigarbha Bodhisattva
domain: Great Vows, Deliverance of Departed Souls, Salvation from Hell
description: 'Not until the hells are emptied will I become a Buddha; not until all beings are saved will I attain enlightenment' — the one bold enough to make that vow is Kshitigarbha Bodhisattva, the Earth Store Bodhisattva, honored in folk belief as Lord of the Underworld and counted among the four great bodhisattvas of Chinese Buddhism, where he embodies the perfection of the Great Vow. His image is easy to spot: a monk's form crowned with a five-leaf Vairocana cap, one hand holding a ringed khakkhara staff that shakes open the gates of hell, the other cradling a luminous pearl that lights the underworld. In Taiwan his role is unusually far-reaching — he is at once a Buddhist bodhisattva and a figure woven deep into Ghost Month rites, ancestor worship, and funerals. Every seventh lunar month, temples and Kshitigarbha halls hold one salvation ceremony after another, and when someone in the family dies, inviting monks to chant the Kshitigarbha Sutra to transfer merit to the departed is something countless Taiwanese families have lived through. When you long to do something for a loved one who has passed, he is the first one most people turn to.
story:
The Kshitigarbha Sutra tells that in a distant age, Kshitigarbha was once a Brahmin woman whose mother had slandered the Three Jewels and fallen into hell after death. The daughter sold off her property, made lavish offerings, and vowed before the Buddha: if her mother could be freed from the torments of hell, she would save all beings, and would not become a Buddha until hell itself was empty. By the power of that vow she rescued not only her mother but set herself on the path of delivering the underworld. In another lifetime, as a girl named Bright Eyes, she again made offerings and vows for a mother fallen into hell. Both stories begin with saving one's mother — filial love bearing up the heaviest vow in all of Buddhism.

Legend adds that in the Tang dynasty a Korean prince of Silla, Kim Gyo-gak, crossed the sea to practice austerities on Mount Jiuhua in China. After his death his body remained incorrupt, his face lifelike, and people took him for a manifestation of Kshitigarbha; Jiuhua became his sacred seat, ranked alongside Putuo, Wutai, and Emei as one of the four great Buddhist mountains. In the Ming and Qing, the Kshitigarbha faith crossed to Taiwan with the migrants and met the island's own deep care for the dead — and here he became a bodhisattva that every household knows.

temples.name: Xinzhuang Dizang An
temples.deityStory: Xinzhuang Dizang An is a famous temple in the north, dedicated to Ksitigarbha and the Dazhong Ye. Known for finding lost items and exorcism, and for its 'Guan Jiang Shou' troupe.

temples.name: Hualien Xiangde Temple
temples.deityStory: Located in Taroko Gorge, it features a towering 36-foot golden statue of Kshitigarbha standing amidst the mountains, protecting the region.

associatedTemples: Xinzhuang Dizang An (Xinzhuang District, New Taipei City)
Manka Dizang An (Wanhua District, Taipei City)
Tianxiang Xiangde Temple (Xiulin Township, Hualien County)
worship: Worship Kshitigarbha with vegetarian offerings — fresh flowers, fruit, clear tea, and cakes — while meat, alcohol, and tobacco are all taboo. The main practice is chanting the Kshitigarbha Sutra or reciting his name, 'Namo Kshitigarbha Bodhisattva.' What sets his worship apart is that so much of it is done on behalf of the dead: when an elder passes, inviting monks to chant the Kshitigarbha Sutra and dedicate the merit is the most common rite in a Taiwanese Buddhist funeral, and the salvation ceremonies held at Kshitigarbha halls and temples through the seventh lunar month are offered for wandering spirits and generations of ancestors alike. There is a place for the living too: you can light a lamp of light to pray for peace and wisdom, and some temples fold the 'settling Tai Sui' ritual into his worship. When you want to do something for a departed loved one, a Kshitigarbha temple is the place to go.
festivals: Kshitigarbha's birthday on the 30th day of the 7th lunar month (the last day of Ghost Month) is the main celebration. This timing is significant — as the "King of the Underworld," his birthday marks the closing of the ghost gates. Temples hold elaborate ceremonies to guide wandering spirits back to the underworld. Xinzhuang Dizang An's Ghost Month activities, including the famous "Night Patrol" by the Guan Jiang Shou troupe, are among the most dramatic religious events in northern Taiwan. Buddhist temples nationwide hold "Yulanpen" (Obon) ceremonies, combining Buddhist teachings with Taiwanese folk traditions of honoring ancestors.

name: Medicine Buddha
domain: Healing, Longevity, Removing Calamities, Physical and Mental Health
description: Every Lunar New Year, Taiwan's Buddhist temples fill with people queuing to light lamps — and more often than not, they're Medicine Buddha lamps, lit in prayer for a whole year free of illness and misfortune for the family. The one entrusted with our health is the Medicine Buddha, Bhaisajyaguru, whose full title is the Medicine Master and Lapis Lazuli Radiance Tathagata, also called the Great Medicine King Buddha. He is the teacher of the Eastern Pure Land of Lapis Lazuli, and together with Amitabha and Shakyamuni he forms the 'Three Buddhas of the Three Ages.' Before he attained Buddhahood he made Twelve Great Vows — from 'curing illness and bringing ease' to granting good food and fine clothing — every one of them aimed at the stuff of ordinary daily life: a sound body, a livable life, a settled heart. That is why the Medicine Buddha is the Buddha Taiwanese most often turn to for recovery from sickness, protection from calamity, and a longer life. When a family member falls ill or a parent grows old, lighting a lamp at the Medicine Buddha hall is something many Taiwanese households do year after year.
story:
The Medicine Buddha Sutra recounts that countless ages ago, while he was still a bodhisattva, the Medicine Buddha made twelve great vows, each aimed squarely at the most concrete of human sufferings: illness that clings to the body, the want of food and clothing, and unrest of body and mind. When every one of those vows was fulfilled, he became a Buddha and established the Eastern Pure Land of Lapis Lazuli — a realm without sickness and without lack. His two attendants are the Bodhisattva of Sunlight and the Bodhisattva of Moonlight, and the three together are called the 'Three Sages of the East,' a mirror to the 'Three Sages of the West' in Amitabha's Pure Land: one land receives the dying, the other looks after this present life.

When the Medicine Buddha faith reached Taiwan, its focus on the here and now — health, family, livelihood — let it blend quickly into everyday life. Today, every New Year from Fo Guang Shan to Dharma Drum Mountain, the lines to light Medicine Buddha lamps and lamps of light stretch on and on, and many temples combine the 'settling Tai Sui' rite with the lamp offering. You could say that most Taiwanese have never read the Medicine Buddha Sutra — and yet nearly every family has, in some way, received his care.

temples.name: Major Buddhist Monasteries
temples.deityStory: Usually enshrined in the Main Hall or Medicine Buddha Hall of major monasteries like Fo Guang Shan and Dharma Drum Mountain.

associatedTemples: Fo Guang Shan (Dashu District, Kaohsiung City)
Dharma Drum Mountain (Jinshan District, New Taipei City)
worship: Offer the Medicine Buddha vegetarian food, keeping meat, alcohol, and tobacco off the altar. The main practice is chanting the Medicine Buddha Sutra and his mantra, or reciting his name, 'Namo Disaster-Dispelling, Life-Extending Medicine Buddha.' The most distinctly Taiwanese ritual is lighting Medicine Buddha lamps: from New Year through the Lantern Festival, temples open their lamp registers, and families dedicate lamps — individual or for the whole household — praying for a year of averted misfortune and extended life. Those who have 'offended Tai Sui' often settle that at the same time, and the large temples like Fo Guang Shan and Dharma Drum Mountain offer the full service. When someone in the family is ill, pray to the Medicine Buddha and see a proper doctor both — 'tending the illness and honoring the divine together' is old Taiwanese wisdom. Bowing to the Buddha isn't a substitute for medicine; it's a way to settle the heart first.
festivals: The Medicine Buddha's birthday is celebrated on the 30th day of the 9th lunar month. Major Buddhist monasteries hold multi-day "Medicine Buddha Dharma Assemblies" featuring group sutra chanting, lamp lighting, and vegetarian feasts. Devotees light "longevity lamps" (Chang Ming Deng) at the altar, praying for health for themselves and their families. Fo Guang Shan and Dharma Drum Mountain host the largest celebrations, often extending over several days with lectures on Buddhist medicine and wellness practices that bridge traditional faith with modern health awareness.

name: Maitreya Buddha
domain: Joy and Contentment, The Future Buddha, Tolerance and Generosity
description: The chubby monk at the temple gate — bare belly, eyes crinkled into happy slits — is someone everyone recognizes. This is Maitreya Buddha, the Big-Belly Maitreya, the Laughing Buddha, whom folk tradition simply calls Budai, the Cloth-Sack Monk. What many people don't realize is his formal role: the 'Future Buddha.' The scriptures prophesy that once the teachings of Shakyamuni have faded from the world, Maitreya will descend, be reborn on earth, attain Buddhahood, and deliver countless beings; until then he remains Maitreya Bodhisattva, dwelling in Tushita Heaven and awaiting the right time. Taiwanese love him for the couplet that hangs beside so many of his statues — 'a belly vast enough to hold all that is hard to bear, a smile wide enough to laugh at all the world's absurdities.' However hard life gets, one look at that laughing face and it starts to feel survivable. That's why his crinkle-eyed image turns up everywhere, from temple gates to shop counters.
story: The Maitreya faith springs from the Maitreya Ascent and Descent Sutras, which describe how Maitreya Bodhisattva now dwells in Tushita Heaven and will, in the far future, descend to be reborn and become the next Buddha after Shakyamuni. But that beloved laughing face comes from a real man — Qici, the Cloth-Sack Monk of the Later Liang during the Five Dynasties. This portly monk wandered from town to town, grinning all day, a great cloth sack slung over his shoulder, telling everyone he met: 'I have a cloth sack, empty as space and free of all hindrance.' No one thought much of him — until, just before he died, he left behind a verse: 'Maitreya, the true Maitreya, dividing into a billion forms, time and again showing himself to the people of the world, yet the people of the world do not know him.' Only then did everyone suddenly understand: the slighted fat monk had been Maitreya all along. From that day on, images of Maitreya in China and Taiwan were no longer the crowned bodhisattva of the Indian scriptures but that sack-toting, ever-laughing monk. The story leaves us a gentle reminder: a Buddha may be standing right beside you, and you simply don't recognize him.

temples.name: Linkou Zhulinshan Guanyin Temple
temples.deityStory: While primarily dedicated to Guanyin, Zhulinshan Guanyin Temple also enshrines Maitreya Buddha. The temple is one of the most popular religious centers in northern Taiwan, with throngs of devotees visiting year-round.

temples.name: Changhua Baguashan Great Buddha Temple
temples.deityStory: Although the iconic hilltop Great Buddha statue depicts Shakyamuni, the temple complex also houses a Maitreya shrine. The Great Buddha is Changhua's most famous landmark, and visitors can climb inside for panoramic views of the Changhua Plain.

associatedTemples: Zhulinshan Guanyin Temple (Linkou, New Taipei City)
Baguashan Great Buddha Temple (Changhua City, Changhua County)
worship: Come to Maitreya with a joyful heart. The offerings are mainly fresh flowers and fruit — keep it simple. Some temples set candy before his statue for visitors to take, a symbol of sharing happiness: take a piece, and remember to walk away smiling. What to pray for? Breadth of heart, an easy mind, the ability to let go. When work is jammed and your chest feels tight, look at that great belly and remind yourself that it can hold anything. Those who formally follow the Maitreya path recite the Maitreya Ascent Sutra and vow to be reborn in Tushita Heaven. His birthday falls on the first day of the first lunar month — New Year's Day itself — so after the New Year's Eve bell-ringing, temples hold his birthday service at dawn on the first morning of the year: the very first lesson of the new year is to keep a smile on your face.
festivals: Maitreya Buddha's birthday falls on the 1st day of the 1st lunar month — New Year's Day itself — signifying the idea of greeting each new year with a joyful heart. After the temple bell-ringing ceremonies on New Year's Eve, major Buddhist monasteries hold Maitreya birthday services at dawn on the first day of the year, blessing all who attend with good fortune for the months ahead.

name: Manjushri Bodhisattva
domain: Supreme Wisdom, Academic Achievement, Eloquence and Insight
description: When exam season arrives, the offering tables at temples enshrining Manjushri pile up with photocopied admission tickets, stacked like a little mountain. Manjushri Bodhisattva — also called Manjusri or the Great Wisdom Manjushri — is the bodhisattva of foremost wisdom in Buddhism, serving alongside Samantabhadra as one of the two attendants of Shakyamuni Buddha; together they form the 'Three Sages of the Avatamsaka.' His attributes are unforgettable: in his right hand he raises the sword of wisdom — which cuts down not enemies but afflictions — in his left he holds the Prajnaparamita sutra, and beneath him rides a blue lion, symbolizing the fierce, untamable power of wisdom. In Taiwan he is the guardian of students and exam-takers, and praying to him for clarity and success before a major test is a fixed ritual for many families. But Manjushri governs more than exams: what he grants is the capacity to think a thing all the way through, and the tangles of life can be brought to him too.
story: Manjushri holds an astonishingly high place in Buddhist scripture. In the Avatamsaka Sutra he is the teacher who first inspires the youth Sudhana, sending him off with a single word on his legendary pilgrimage to fifty-three teachers. In the Vimalakirti Sutra the story is even better: when the formidable layman Vimalakirti fell ill and the Buddha asked his disciples to visit, one after another begged off — Vimalakirti's eloquence was so keen that whoever went would be left tongue-tied. In the end only Manjushri accepted, and the meeting of those two brilliant minds produced one of the most celebrated dialogues on truth in all of Buddhism. The scriptures also let slip a secret: Manjushri in fact attained Buddhahood long ago — as the 'Dragon-Seed Sovereign King Buddha' in a past age and as the 'Universally-Seeing Tathagata' in an age to come — and chose to turn back and appear in a bodhisattva's form to guide beings toward awakening. Mount Wutai in China is revered as his sacred seat, drawing pilgrims and eminent monks for centuries; and when this faith in wisdom reached Taiwan with Buddhism, it became the firmest support of the island's exam-takers.

temples.name: Hsinchu Puxian Temple
temples.deityStory: Puxian Temple enshrines both Manjushri and Samantabhadra, making it a vital destination for students in the Hsinchu area seeking blessings for exams. During testing season, the temple fills with students and parents praying for wisdom and success.

associatedTemples: Hsinchu Puxian Temple (Hsinchu City)
worship: Offerings to Manjushri have a special twist: alongside fresh flowers and fruit, you may offer stationery — pens and books are both welcome. Exam-takers most often bring a copy of their admission ticket or the pen they'll write with to be blessed before the altar, praying for a clear head on the day and a place at the top of the list. Practitioners of his path chant the Manjushri Heart Mantra ('Om A Ra Pa Ca Na Dhih') or recite the Manjushri Prajnaparamita Sutra. His birthday falls on the 4th day of the fourth lunar month, when temples hold wisdom-themed Dharma assemblies, and around exam season many temples light 'wisdom lamps.' One reminder: Manjushri grants wisdom, not answers — you still have to read the books yourself. What he blesses is your ability to take them in.
festivals: Manjushri Bodhisattva's birthday is celebrated on the 4th day of the 4th lunar month. Major Buddhist temples hold wisdom-themed Dharma assemblies and blessing ceremonies. Many temples near schools also organize 'Wisdom Lamp' services around exam season, allowing students to light lamps before Manjushri's image as they pray for academic success.

name: Samantabhadra Bodhisattva
domain: Great Vows in Action, Diligent Practice, Upholding the Dharma
description: Each of Buddhism's four great bodhisattvas has a specialty: Guanyin embodies compassion, Manjushri wisdom, Kshitigarbha the great vow — and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, also called the All-Pervading Goodness or the Great-Practice Samantabhadra, embodies action: actually carrying the Dharma into practice. The Avatamsaka Sutra honors him as the 'eldest son of all Buddhas,' and with Manjushri he flanks Shakyamuni left and right as one of the 'Three Sages of the Avatamsaka' — where Manjushri represents thinking a thing through, Samantabhadra represents getting it done. His image is easy to know: he rides a white six-tusked elephant, the six tusks standing for the six paramitas — giving, discipline, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom. In Taiwan his worship is not as widespread as that of Guanyin or Kshitigarbha, but his 'Ten Great Vows' serve as the daily blueprint of practice for countless Buddhist disciples at their morning and evening devotions. Those who know say it plainly: to worship Samantabhadra is to worship the principle of 'don't just talk about it — do it.'
story: The finale of the Avatamsaka Sutra belongs to Samantabhadra. In the chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm, the youth Sudhana visits fifty-three teachers — Guanyin and Maitreya among them — and only when he reaches Samantabhadra at the very end does his quest come to completion. The destination of the seeker's journey turns out to be not some loftier theory, but simply: to act. Legend says that countless ages ago Samantabhadra made a vast vow to help all beings accomplish Buddhahood through 'great practice,' and his Ten Great Vows — from paying homage to all Buddhas and repenting past misdeeds to accommodating all beings and dedicating every merit — break the whole of practice down into ten things a person can actually do. His white six-tusked elephant, drawn from Indian tradition, stands for noble, pure, steady strength: an elephant plants each foot firmly, just as practice must. Mount Emei in Sichuan has long been revered as his sacred seat, ranked with Putuo, Wutai, and Jiuhua among the four great Buddhist mountains. In the Sui and Tang, eminent monks of the Tiantai and Huayan schools placed special weight on his teaching of the Ten Vows, and in the Ming and Qing the faith reached Taiwan, where it continues to this day.

temples.name: Hsinchu Puxian Temple
temples.deityStory: Puxian Temple takes its name from Samantabhadra (Puxian in Chinese) and is one of the rare Taiwanese temples that enshrines him as the principal deity. The temple houses an elegant statue of Samantabhadra seated atop a white elephant, exuding serene majesty.

associatedTemples: Hsinchu Puxian Temple (Hsinchu City)
worship: Worship Samantabhadra with vegetarian offerings — fresh flowers, fruit, clear tea — avoiding meat, alcohol, and tobacco. The chant of first choice is the chapter on the Practices and Vows of Samantabhadra from the Avatamsaka Sutra, or his name, 'Namo Great-Practice Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.' But the true heart of his worship isn't on the offering table — it's off it. The Ten Great Vows are meant to be done: pay homage to the Buddhas each day, rejoice when you see others do good, repent honestly when you slip, dedicate your merit to all beings. Many disciples keep these ten vows as a daily checklist, fulfilling them one at a time. What to pray for? Follow-through, and a resolve that doesn't fade — anyone whose plans forever stall at step one has much to learn from this most action-minded of bodhisattvas. His birthday falls on the 21st day of the second lunar month, when temples hold sutra-chanting assemblies.
festivals: Samantabhadra Bodhisattva's birthday is celebrated on the 21st day of the 2nd lunar month. Buddhist temples hold special Dharma assemblies where the congregation recites the chapter on the Practices and Vows of Samantabhadra together, reaffirming their commitment to translating the Dharma into action through the Ten Great Vows.

name: Skanda Bodhisattva
domain: Buddhist Protector, Temple Guardian, Exorciser of Evil
description: Walk into a Taiwanese Buddhist temple and the first figure to greet you at the gate is the beaming Maitreya; turn around, and there stands a warrior in golden armor gripping a vajra staff, facing the main hall. This is Skanda Bodhisattva, also called Wei Tuo Tian or General Wei, the most famous Dharma-protector in Chinese Buddhism. Maitreya faces outward to welcome visitors while Skanda faces inward to guard them — 'enter and meet Maitreya, turn and see Skanda' is the traditional layout of the Hall of Heavenly Kings. His duty is to protect the Dharma, defend the monastery, and subdue the armies of demons. Those in the know read one telling detail: the way Skanda holds his vajra staff signals the temple's lodging rules. Laid flat across both forearms, it welcomes traveling monks to stay three days; held upright at the waist, one day; and resting point-down on the ground, it means, regretfully, no lodging here. Next time you pass through a temple's mountain gate, remember to glance back at this silent sentinel general.
story:
Skanda's most famous legend is the tale of the swift demon and the Buddha's tooth. After the Buddha's parinirvana, the story goes, the gods gathered beneath the twin sala trees to receive his tooth relic. In the grief and distraction of the moment, a swift-footed demon darted in, snatched the tooth, and fled. The instant Skanda heard, he threw on his golden armor, took up his precious staff, and gave chase — and however fast and far the demon ran, Skanda never fell behind, until at last he recovered the tooth and returned it to the stupa. From then on he was honored as a Dharma-protector: whenever the true teaching is threatened, he pursues to the very end.

Another account traces Skanda back to the Indian war god Kumara, originally a many-faced, many-armed deity riding a peacock. As Buddhism spread east, he was reshaped into a refined yet formidable Chinese general; his place in the Hall of Heavenly Kings was fixed after the Song dynasty, and the faith came to Taiwan with Buddhism in the Ming and Qing. Behind the gates of Taiwan's temples, this general who has given chase for a thousand years still stands guard.

temples.name: Chung Tai Chan Monastery
temples.deityStory: The Skanda statue at Chung Tai Chan Monastery is a granite masterpiece, showcasing the dignity and power of the protector.

associatedTemples: Chung Tai Chan Monastery (Puli Township, Nantou County)
Major Buddhist monasteries nationwide
worship: Skanda is a guardian of the monastery, not a wish-granting counter — devotees rarely ask him for wealth or romance, and instead pray for progress in their practice, for not backsliding, and for the protection of the Dharma. Offerings are mainly vegetarian; you may light a pure lamp and chant the Heart Sutra or the Skanda mantra. Buddhist practitioners often pay their respects to Skanda before taking refuge or receiving the precepts, as a sign that they are ready to accept the Dharma's guidance and protection. When you visit the great monasteries — Fo Guang Shan, Dharma Drum Mountain, Chung Tai Chan Monastery — don't forget to pause in the Hall of Heavenly Kings and see how Skanda holds his vajra staff. It's the temple's silent notice about lodging for traveling monks, and one of the most delightful details to look for in a Taiwanese Buddhist temple.
festivals: Skanda's commemoration day is the 3rd day of the 6th lunar month. While not as widely celebrated as major Buddhist holidays, monasteries hold special ceremonies honoring all Dharma protectors on this day. The ceremony typically includes sutra chanting, offerings, and a procession around the monastery grounds. Skanda is also prominently featured during the "Thousand Buddha Repentance" (Qian Fo Chan) ceremony, a grand Buddhist ritual held at major temples, where his role as the ultimate protector of Buddhism is emphasized.

name: Sangharama Bodhisattva
domain: Buddhist Protector, Temple Guardian, Symbol of Loyalty
description: You may not know it, but Lord Guan goes by another name inside a Buddhist temple. Sangharama Bodhisattva — also called the Venerable Sangharama — is the monastery-guardian deity of Chinese Buddhism, and his most famous manifestation is none other than Guan Yu, the Three Kingdoms general also worshipped as Guan Sheng Di Jun. 'Sangharama' originally meant the pure monastic grounds where monks dwell, and the Sangharama Bodhisattva is the guardian of those grounds. Legend says that after Guan Yu died in battle, he was awakened and took refuge under Master Zhiyi of the Tiantai school, and from then on stood watch over Buddhist temples as a protector. In a Chinese Buddhist temple he is placed symmetrically with Skanda, one within and one without — 'Skanda subdues demons on the outside, Sangharama guards the temple within.' So the very same Guan Gong carries a double identity in Taiwan: in a Guan Emperor temple he is the Martial Sage and a god of wealth, while in a temple's Sangharama hall he is a Dharma-protector. Next time you catch sight of that familiar red face in the rear hall of Longshan Temple, you'll understand — here, he is on duty for the Buddha.
story:
Legend has it that in the last years of the Eastern Han, after Guan Yu was defeated at Maicheng and beheaded by the forces of Eastern Wu, his spirit would not disperse and often appeared around Jingzhou. One night it drifted to Mount Yuquan in Hubei, where Master Zhiyi of the Tiantai school was cultivating in the hills, and Guan Yu roared out: 'Give me back my head!' The master calmly answered: 'General, in life you killed countless men — from whom should all their heads be demanded?' The words struck like a thunderclap. Guan Yu saw all at once how heavy his own karma of killing was, repented on the spot, took refuge, received the precepts, and became a Dharma-protector — the Sangharama Bodhisattva, appearing at Mount Yuquan to guard the teaching.

The story first appears in Song-dynasty Buddhist histories. The dates don't line up with history — Master Zhiyi was born more than three centuries after Guan Yu — but it remains one of the most elegant strokes in the sinicization of Buddhism: welcoming the Han people's most revered Martial Sage into the fold as a guardian. In the Ming and Qing the belief crossed to Taiwan with the migrants, giving the island its distinctive sight of one god with two names, honored by Buddhists and Taoists alike.

temples.name: Fo Guang Shan
temples.deityStory: Fo Guang Shan has a Sangharama Hall beside the Main Hall, enshrining Guan Yu, corresponding with Skanda to protect the monastery.

associatedTemples: Major Buddhist monasteries nationwide
worship: Worshipping the Sangharama Bodhisattva follows the customs of the Buddhist temple: vegetarian offerings, and chanting the Heart Sutra and the Great Compassion Mantra, or reciting his name, 'Namo Sangharama Holy Assembly Bodhisattva.' As a monastery guardian, he is mostly asked for smooth practice and a thriving temple rather than personal worldly affairs. The fascinating part is that changing the setting changes the way you pray: the very same Guan Gong is the Martial Sage, a god of wealth, and a god of loyalty in a Guan Emperor temple, where you may pray for career and prosperity — and a Dharma-protector in a Buddhist Sangharama hall, where you pray for the protection of the teaching. What you can ask for depends on which kind of temple you've stepped into, and that flexibility is exactly what makes Taiwanese belief so distinctive. On his birthday, the 13th of the fifth lunar month, Buddhist temples and Guan Emperor temples often hold celebrations on the same day, the Buddhist and Taoist sides rejoicing together.
festivals: Guan Yu's birthday on the 24th day of the 6th lunar month is celebrated in both Buddhist monasteries and folk temples across Taiwan. In Buddhist settings, monks hold Dharma assemblies honoring his vow to protect Buddhism. In folk religion, the celebration is much grander — major temples like Xingtian Temple in Taipei see enormous crowds, with elaborate processions and theatrical performances reenacting the "Romance of the Three Kingdoms." Xingtian Temple's celebration is one of the largest in Taiwan, reflecting Guan Yu's extraordinary popularity as a deity who transcends religious boundaries.

name: Acala (Fudo Myoo)
domain: Vanquishing Demons and Obstacles, Unwavering Resolve, Protection of Practitioners
description: A body of blue-green, eyes glaring wide, flames roaring up behind him — first-time visitors are often taken aback: a Buddhist protector looks like this? This is Acala, known in Japanese as Fudo Myoo and in Chinese as Budong Mingwang, the foremost of the Five Wisdom Kings of Esoteric Buddhism. A 'Wisdom King' is neither Buddha nor bodhisattva but the wrathful form the Buddhas manifest to subdue beings too stubborn and hardened for gentle words — and Acala is precisely the emanation of Mahavairocana Buddha (Dainichi Nyorai). His right hand grips a demon-quelling sword that severs affliction, his left a lasso that draws suffering beings back to the path, and he stands immovably on a great boulder, a symbol of resolve that never retreats; the fire blazing behind him burns not people but karmic defilements. Acala worship followed a distinctive road in Taiwan: it came mainly through Japanese Buddhism (the Shingon school and others) during the colonial era rather than the Chinese tradition, and to this day it centers on the temples of northern Taiwan where Japanese influence ran deepest, such as Beitou's Puji Temple. It's a niche faith — but its story runs deep.
story:
In Esoteric teaching, when Mahavairocana Buddha faces beings whom even the gentlest face cannot persuade, he changes that face — manifesting as the wrathful Acala. His fury is not true anger but the thunderclap of compassion: some people are so deeply lost that they must be jolted awake. The two characters of his name, 'the Immovable,' hold the essence — not standing physically still, but a heart unmoved by external circumstance: however great the temptation, terror, or suffering before it, the resolve for the Way stays firm as bedrock and does not retreat a single step.

The three great masters of the Tang's Kaiyuan era — Subhakarasimha, Vajrabodhi, and Amoghavajra — brought the Esoteric teachings to China, and Japan's Master Kukai (Kobo Daishi) carried them home to found the Shingon school. Acala went on to become one of Japan's most revered protectors, above all the steadfast pillar for the mountain ascetics of Shugendo as they faced physical peril and inner demons alike. During the colonial period the faith crossed to Taiwan, leaving its mark around Taipei and Keelung — Beitou's Puji Temple survives as one such Japanese-style Buddhist temple. After the war, Chinese Buddhism became the mainstream, but Acala never disappeared; he stands quietly within the Esoteric circle of practice, as unshaken as the boulder beneath his feet.

temples.name: Taipei Beitou Puji Temple
temples.deityStory: Built in 1905 during the Japanese colonial period, Puji Temple was originally a Shingon Buddhist temple called Tesshinzan. It retains its Japanese architectural style to this day and is designated a Taipei City historic site. The temple enshrines Acala as its principal deity and is one of Taiwan's few well-preserved Japanese-era Buddhist temples.

associatedTemples: Beitou Puji Temple (Beitou, Taipei City)
worship: Worshipping Acala in Taiwan takes two forms. In a Chinese Buddhist temple: vegetarian offerings and the chanting of Acala's heart mantra, a practice common among lay Esoteric devotees. In a Japanese Esoteric setting, the most distinctive rite is the 'Goma' fire ritual — wishes are written on goma wood and cast into a sacred fire altar to burn, symbolizing flames that consume karmic obstacles and carry the devotee's vows up to the Buddhas; full Goma ceremonies are rare in Taiwan, seen mostly at large Esoteric assemblies. What to pray for? Acala governs the act of holding on: when your will is weak, when you're ready to give up in the face of obstacles, when you need to break a bad habit, he is the one to ask for firm resolve and unwavering practice. Japanese tradition keeps the 28th of each month as 'Acala's day,' and some Taiwanese practitioners still observe it by reciting his mantra and sitting in meditation.
festivals: Acala's birthday is observed on the 28th day of the 9th lunar month. Temples that enshrine him hold Goma fire rituals (homa) — sacred ceremonies in which a consecrated fire, representing Acala's wisdom-flames, is used to burn wooden prayer tablets inscribed with the wishes of devotees, carrying their aspirations to the heavens.
